clinicalPearls: A benign functional disorder of young infants, typically under nine months, marked by prolonged screaming, crying and straining with facial reddening that precedes passage of a soft stool.
The episodes reflect failure to coordinate a Valsalva effort with relaxation of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter, not obstruction or hard stool.
The stool that is eventually passed is soft or normal in consistency, which is the key feature distinguishing dyschezia from constipation.
Crying stops immediately once the stool is passed, and the infant is otherwise well and thriving.
It is a Rome IV functional gastrointestinal disorder of infancy; the diagnosis is clinical from a typical history in a well infant.
Reassurance and parental education are the mainstay; no medication or dietary change is required.
Rectal or digital stimulation and suppositories should be avoided as they may create a harmful conditioned response and delay learning of normal defecation.
Symptoms resolve once the infant learns to coordinate defecation, usually within a few weeks.
reference.pathophysiology: Infant dyschezia arises from immaturity of the coordination between the rise in intra-abdominal pressure generated by the infant through crying, straining and Valsalva, and the reflex relaxation of the pelvic floor and external anal sphincter required to permit stool passage. Because the infant cannot yet synchronise these events, effective evacuation is delayed and considerable straining and crying occur, even though the stool is soft and the rectum is not obstructed. There is no structural, neuromuscular or metabolic abnormality; the phenomenon represents normal maturation of the defecation reflex and resolves as the infant learns the appropriate coordination.
additionalDifferentials: Functional constipation (stools are hard rather than soft)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination including inspection of the perineum and anal position and patency
Documentation of stool consistency (soft stool supports the diagnosis)
Digital rectal examination if a structural anomaly or Hirschsprung disease is suspected
Contrast studies or rectal suction biopsy reserved for suspected Hirschsprung disease or anatomical anomaly
redFlags: Passage of hard stools, or delayed passage of meconium at birth suggesting constipation or Hirschsprung disease
Faltering growth, abdominal distension or bilious vomiting
Abnormal anal position, an imperforate or stenotic anus, or an absent anal wink on examination
Symptoms beginning after nine months of age or persisting well beyond infancy
reference.prognosis: Excellent; a self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously within weeks to a few months as the infant matures and learns to coordinate defecation, with no long-term sequelae.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as constipation and prescribing laxatives despite the stools being soft.
Recommending rectal stimulation or suppositories, which can establish a conditioned dependence.
Overlooking an anorectal anomaly by omitting inspection of the perineum.
Failing to reassure parents, prompting unnecessary investigation and anxiety.
Confusing the straining with pain arising from an anal fissure.
references: Rome IV criteria for functional gastrointestinal disorders (neonate and toddler)
management: Reassurance and parental education that this is benign and resolves as the infant learns to coordinate defecation
Avoidance of rectal stimulation with suppositories or digital manoeuvres, which may interfere with the infant learning the normal reflex
No medication or dietary change, as neither laxatives nor formula changes are required
Confirmation of normal growth and soft stool consistency to support the diagnosis
Safety-netting to review if the stool becomes hard, growth falters or other concerning features develop
